metadata.title: Michigan Democrat William Lawrence Faces Scrutiny Over Deleted Social Media Posts

sources.news_title: The posts include support for police and prison abolition, calls to nationalize fossil fuels and attacks on moderate Democrats, raising concerns in a battleground district.
sources.text:
A Democrat nominee for a competitive Michigan House seat, William Lawrence, deleted hundreds of social media posts calling for far-left policies before launching his campaign.
These posts included supporting the abolition of core institutions, including the police and prisons, the Senate, and even called for a “fundamental overhaul” of the Constitution, CNN reported Friday. (RELATED: Somehow Voters Still Hate Democrats More Than Republicans)
Lawrence had also said “f*ck” the nuclear family and called it an “isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society.”
Other posts include calling for the nationalization of fossil-fuel companies so that they can be forced to end production, and sharing that he envisioned a “world of free and open migration.”
EXCLUSIVE
Michigan Congressional candidate William Lawrence says kids should get s*x change surgeries
A concerned citizen asked him if he thinks kids should be able to get s*x changes. His response?
“I believe that each family should have the freedom to pursue the course of… pic.twitter.com/lfjMxYCKZw
Lawrence had also attacked moderate members of his own party, saying in 2020 that he was “ashamed to be represented” by the then-Rep., now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin, whom he described as a “supposed Democrat” after she did not condemn President Donald Trump’s strike killing Iranian Gen. Qasem Soleimani.
Similar attacks would continue, going as far as writing a song in 2021 that had been inspired by the resistance of Democrat Sen. Joe Manchin to the Democrats’ climate agenda.
The song, titled “Our generation says f*ck you for everything,” included the lyric “Hurry up and die so that we can get started.”
If Lawrence wins this November, he could serve as a deciding vote in the House, taking many of these positions with him. However, Lawrence has since walked some of these positions back.
Voters in MI-07 are wondering where Tom Barrett is.
He doesn’t host real town halls or show up around the district. He avoids and ignores his constituents.
My day 1 priority is top-notch constituent services in the district. I want to represent Mid-Michiganders in Congress, not… pic.twitter.com/wifhL7349L
When some deleted posts about supporting the “defund the police” movement were raised in an interview with Semafor in July, Lawrence said that his comments were “out of step with what I believe now.”
He also told CNN last month that he had let his membership with the Democratic Socialists of America “lapse.” He now tells CNN that he regrets his comments directed at Slotkin and that he no longer supports open borders.
“Like many millennials, I’ve done my fair share of thinking out loud on the internet,” Lawrence told CNN. “I’ve been clear that I disagree today with some things I posted in the past; I remain a staunch critic of the political status quo, and the obscene concentration of wealth and power that corrupts our politics and leaves working people unrepresented.”
Lawrence has now been the Democrat nominee since August and is preparing to dethrone Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, an incumbent fighting in his first reelection campaign.
Polls taken in mid-August and conducted by the House Majority PAC, whose stated goal is to elect House Democrats, show that Lawrence is up two points on Barrett, as the current representative has a 47 percent unfavorable view.
Lawrence responded to the report, saying that “Billionaire-funded SuperPACs are launching attack ads against me,” by digging up old tweets that “I deleted because I didn’t agree with them anymore.”
“I’ve said some dumb things,” Lawrence said. “I don’t take orders from billionaires or party bosses. That’s why these billionaires are going all out to try to defeat me.” (RELATED: Trump’s Ex-Labor Secretary Fancied Strip Clubs, Abused Public Office Investigation Finds)

The Democrat nominee for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District reportedly deleted social media posts where he espoused the abolition of prisons, attacked moderate Democrats, and argued against the nuclear family.
U.S. House candidate William Lawrence took down hundreds of posts supporting leftist causes that included getting rid of police and pushing for a “fundamental overhaul” of the Constitution, CNN reported Friday, noting the posts were from the time when he was a progressive organizer.
The article continued:
Other deleted posts show Lawrence writing “f**k” the nuclear-family home and calling it an “isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society,” envisioning “a world of free and open migration,” and calling to “Abolish the Senate.”
Lawrence even wrote a song inspired by moderate Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin’s resistance to Democrats’ climate agenda: “Our generation says f**k you for everything,” Lawrence wrote in lyrics he posted in December 2021. “Hurry up and die so that we can get started.”
According to CNN senior politics reporter Andrew Kaczynski, Lawrence has since claimed he disagreed with some of the old posts.
However, Lawrence’s statement on the matter appeared to be the leftist candidate’s attempt to simply wipe his record clean prior to the election:
Lawrence was arrested for resisting police officers while protesting the Enbridge Line 5 pipeline in 2013, according to Fox News.
“He and others chained themselves to machinery in protest of the pipeline, which helps the U.S. meet critical energy needs but has also been a subject of pushback by environmental groups and indigenous tribes whose land the pipeline partially runs through,” the outlet said, noting his conviction was later expunged.
Lawrence won the Democrat primary in August and is currently running against incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett (R), per the CNN article.
Breitbart News recently detailed more of Lawrence’s background and Barrett’s record.
“Michigan Democrat congressional candidate William Lawrence, co-founder of the Soros-supported Sunrise Movement, a radical left-wing climate activist organization that describes its mission as ‘fighting fascism to win a Green New Deal,’ called for ‘reconstructing’ America through racial and economic justice in a 2023 interview,” the outlet said.
“Republican Congressman Barrett is a former Army helicopter pilot seeking reelection in Michigan’s Seventh Congressional District, a toss-up seat that voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 and could help determine control of the House. During his time in Congress, Barrett has delivered historic tax cuts for hardworking families and expanded benefits for Michigan veterans,” it stated.

Question: Where do Democrats keep finding radical nominees who have to zero out their entire social-media output in order to run for office?
Answer: Michigan! To be fair, we can probably narrow the answer down to Ann Arbor and Dearbornistan.
Earlier this week, my colleague Matt Vespa published a series of Abdul El-Sayed's tweets about 9/11 that he sent to the memory hole after winning the Democrats' Senate primary in Michigan. Today, CNN's Andrew Kaczynski unearthed even more obnoxious social-media posts from William Lawrence, a Sunrise Movement radical who won the Dems' House primary for MI-07 to challenge first-term incumbent Republican Tom Barrett.
Michigan's 7th CD is a dead-even district in the Cook index, and had been seen as a prime pick-up opportunity ... as long as no nuclear families live in it. Democrats' ambitions for this seat may run into the same problems as their ambitions for the Senate seat, as the K-Files reporter's research reveals Lawrence's true nature:
William Lawrence, the Democratic nominee in one of the country’s most competitive House races in Michigan, deleted hundreds of old social media posts in which he embraced police and prison abolition, called for nationalizing fossil-fuel companies to end their production, attacked moderate Democrats and argued for a “fundamental overhaul” of the Constitution.
Other deleted posts show Lawrence writing “f**k” the nuclear-family home and calling it an “isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society,” envisioning “a world of free and open migration,” and calling to “Abolish the Senate.”
Lawrence even wrote a song inspired by moderate Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin’s resistance to Democrats’ climate agenda: “Our generation says f**k you for everything,” Lawrence wrote in lyrics he posted in December 2021. “Hurry up and die so that we can get started.”
The deleted posts, most of which have not been previously reported and came under a previous Twitter handle, stretch back years to when Lawrence, now 36, was building his career as a progressive organizer as an original co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, helping propel the Green New Deal into Democratic politics in 2018.
Well, let's talk about the Sunrise Movement for a moment. A year ago, the Department of Justice reportedly opened a probe into George Soros' funding of potentially violent radical groups as part of its investigation into Antifa and its funding. The New York Times reported on the effort without mentioning the Sunrise Movement, but the Capital Research Center released its own report into Soros' ties to the violent and radical Left a week prior to the NYT's report, and immediately after the assassination of Charlie Kirk. Ryan Mauro's investigation claimed that Soros' funding went to the Sunrise Movement, a group that fits the FBI definition of "domestic terrorism," as I wrote at the time:
Mauro identifies $23 million in Soros funding that went to groups that participate directly or indirectly in domestic political violence, according to the FBI's definition of the term. Those include:
- Center for Third World Organizing / Ruckus Society / BlackOUT Collective
- Grassroots Global Justice Alliance
- The Sunrise Movement
- Movement for Black Lives & Dream Defenders
- Dissenters
- U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights
The recent declaration by Trump of Antifa as a terrorist organization may have given the DoJ even more interest in this report. Mauro links Sunrise to Antifa activities in Atlanta, specifically Stop Cop City and Defend the Atlanta Forest.
It's not clear what Lawrence did within the Sunrise Movement, but his affiliation with the radical action group speaks volumes. So too does his previous membership in the Democratic Socialists of America. The NYT noted both of these problems after Lawrence won the nomination in a three-way race a month ago, while suggesting that the GOP may have given Lawrence an Akin-esque push to get there:
He does not identify as a democratic socialist, he told The Times, but his campaign has confirmed that he was previously a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. The group has not endorsed him. ...
Mr. Maasdam said that a shadowy super PAC’s ads attacking him and promoting Mr. Lawrence were evidence that Republicans would rather face him than a moderate in the fall. The PAC, called Sunrise Michigan, has not disclosed its donors, but Republican PACs have meddled in a series of Democratic primary races this year. Sunrise Michigan uses a little-known South Dakota bank that has been linked with Republican operatives.
During the campaign, Mr. Lawrence faced backlash over a comment he made in 2024 that an older generation of Black Democratic leadership “defangs the white left.” He said he regretted the remark.
I'll bet he does. Don't expect that comment to help El-Sayed in Detroit, either. And while Maasdam has motives to deflect responsibility for his primary loss, he may not be wrong, either. Democrats pulled this same stunt in 2012's Missouri Senate race by attacking everyone in the GOP primary except Todd Akin, who got set up as an easy foil for Claire McCaskill's surprise reelection. To a certain extent, Democrats and the Protection Racket Media employed the same strategy in 2015 by promoting every move Donald Trump made, carrying his rallies live, and highlighting his attacks on Republican primary opponents. Hillary Clinton believed Trump would be easier to beat, and ... well, let's hope things work out better in MI-07 for the GOP.
On that point, Republicans can be hopeful. As noted above, party affiliation in this district is about even, and so are its electoral results. In 2024, the district barely went in Trump's favor, 50/49, while it also narrowly supported Democrat Elissa Slotkin over Mike Rogers in the Senate race, 49/48. Trump won it in 2016, 49/45, but Joe Biden edged him 5-/49 two years later. In the 2022 midterms, without the effect of Trump being on the ballot, the district trended more Democrat, but Democrats didn't put radicals like El-Sayed and Lawrence on that ballot, either.
In this election, with El-Sayed at the top of the ballot and Lawrence nominated for the House, Republicans can hope for a big turnout and a revulsion at the radical nature of both nominees. Barrett has the advantage of incumbency, albeit muted as a first-term Congressman, but the foul-mouthed DSA alum provides the starkest contrast between a relatively normal status quo and a Marxist revolution as the only other option. Barrett better stick the landing, and Rogers too.

William Lawrence, the Democratic nominee in one of the country’s most competitive House races in Michigan, deleted hundreds of old social media posts in which he embraced police and prison abolition, called for nationalizing fossil-fuel companies to end their production, attacked moderate Democrats and argued for a “fundamental overhaul” of the Constitution.
Other deleted posts show Lawrence writing “f**k” the nuclear-family home and calling it an “isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society,” envisioning “a world of free and open migration,” and calling to “Abolish the Senate.”
Lawrence even wrote a song inspired by moderate Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin’s resistance to Democrats’ climate agenda: “Our generation says f**k you for everything,” Lawrence wrote in lyrics he posted in December 2021. “Hurry up and die so that we can get started.”
The deleted posts, most of which have not been previously reported and came under a previous Twitter handle, stretch back years to when Lawrence, now 36, was building his career as a progressive organizer as an original co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, helping propel the Green New Deal into Democratic politics in 2018.
Since winning the Democratic primary in August, he’s now the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, running against incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, who is seeking to win his first reelection.
Michigan’s 7th is one of the country’s truest House battleground tests: President Donald Trump carried it by less than two points in 2024 and the district was previously represented by now-Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
But Lawrence’s past rhetoric may complicate Democrats’ ability to retake the district, especially those deleted posts which include attacks aimed at fellow Democrats from the party’s more moderate wing, including Slotkin.
In January 2020, Lawrence attacked then-Rep. Slotkin, writing that he was “ashamed to be represented” by her and calling her a “supposed Democrat” over her response to President Donald Trump’s decision to order a deadly strike on Iranian Gen. Qasem Soleimani, saying she did not condemn Trump.
‘Thinking out loud on the internet’
Lawrence has since distanced himself from at least some of his earlier positions. He told Semafor last month that his past posts supporting the 2020 “defund the police” movement “are out of step with what I believe now.” Last month, he told CNN’s Manu Raju that he let his membership in the Democratic Socialists of America “lapse” in July.
He told CNN in a further statement he regretted his past comments on Sen. Slotkin and said he did not support defunding the police or open borders.
“Like many millennials, I’ve done my fair share of thinking out loud on the internet. I’ve been clear that I disagree today with some things I posted in the past. I don’t support defunding the police or open borders. I don’t agree with my previous statement about Senator Slotkin, who has been fiercely critical of the Trump administration’s war in Iran and is doing essential work to protect the integrity of the upcoming election. I remain a staunch critic of the political status quo, and the obscene concentration of wealth and power that corrupts our politics and leaves working people unrepresented.
He’s one of a number of progressive candidates this cycle to face scrutiny over a scrubbed social-media history. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, has faced criticism over deleted posts supporting the “defund the police” movement, as well as since-removed YouTube videos in which he suggested football was racist.
Also in Michigan, El-Sayed’s one-time rival for the Democratic Senate nomination Mallory McMorrow suspended her campaign months after CNN reported that she had deleted thousands of old tweets.
            In Wisconsin, democratic socialist Francesca Hong lost her gubernatorial primary after her deleted posts uncovered by CNN became a late issue in the race, while in New York City, DSA-backed Darializa Avila Chevalier upset longtime Rep. Adriano Espaillat after CNN uncovered a deleted account containing calls to abolish police, prisons and borders and embraces of communisms.
    
‘A world without police and prisons’
Lawrence’s ideological arguments stretched well beyond Democratic infighting.
In 2021, Lawrence praised the Minneapolis activist group Black Visions, writing that its ‘defund the police’ campaign had brought the country “nearer to a world without police and prisons.”
In August 2022, he argued that remaining fossil-fuel production should be wound down through a “more confrontational” strategy, writing that it “should happen through forced nationalization and that should be our demand.” In October 2021, he pushed for then-President Joe Biden to “promise” to “end the coal industry,” through an executive order.
Later in August 2022, Lawrence summarized his politics as “social democrat in the streets, libertarian socialist in the sheets.”
He repeatedly took aim at the nuclear family home as well.
“F**k isolation and the nuclear family domicile,” Lawrence wrote in 2021 while praising communal living. The following year, he went further, calling the nuclear-family home an “isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society.” “I don’t want to be part of that,” he wrote.
Days later, Lawrence argued that the “hetero-patriarchial nuclear family” is a “MATERIAL foundation of wealth accumulation” because inheritance was concentrated through male family lines, while writing that “Queer families create MATERIAL conditions for solidarity and wealth sharing.”
His critiques extended to America’s political and economic order more broadly.
On Indigenous Peoples’ Day in 2020, Lawrence thanked indigenous writers and organizers who he said helped him “imagine a world beyond the nation-state and capitalism.”
“May the 21st century begin an indigenous millennium,” he wrote.
In another post, Lawrence declared: “Racial capitalism is the problem. Empire is the problem.”
And in 2021 he urged readers to “envision a world of free and open migration,” answering his own question — “You mean, ANYBODY can move ANYWHERE??” — with an emphatic: “Yes!”
Attacks on moderates
Many of Lawrence’s now deleted posts were also attacks aimed at more moderate members of the Democratic Party.
Following the 2020 election, when Democratic then-Rep. Abigail Spanberger criticized “defund the police” and socialist rhetoric, Lawrence dismissed her comments as a “tantrum” and warned that “timid Dems” could “leave the Party” if they could not accept the activist left.
In another intra-party fight over President Biden’s Build Back Better agenda, Lawrence warned that if the bill failed to pass the House, he urged progressives to go “scorched earth” on conservative Democrats and the “absolute rubes throughout the party who believed them.”
Months later, responding to a moderate account, he wrote, “You f**king morons,” for questioning why Republicans overturned Roe. v. Wade before the 2022 midterm elections.
Lawrence also questioned whether Democrats should seek broad governing majorities at all if it meant sacrificing their values.
He wrote that it was “better to be a minority party that stands for something than a majority party that can’t govern,” arguing that it was sometimes necessary “to divide in order to unite a stronger and more coherent force.” In another post, he declared: “It’s time for the Dem civil war to rage.”
